notes.front: In a flared tube fitting, what does the flare do?
notes.back: The tube’s flared end is drawn by the sleeve and nut tightly against a male fitting to form a seal.
notes.explanation: The male fitting has a cone-shaped surface with the same angle as the inside of the flare, so tubing must be flared before installation.
notes.example: Like the widened mouth of a trumpet pressed onto a matching cone, with a nut behind it clamping the two together.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “AN Flared Fittings”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: The nut fits over the sleeve and, when tightened, draws the sleeve and tubing flare tightly against a male fitting to form a seal. Tubing used with this type of fitting must be flared before installation.

notes.front: What are flareless fittings, and what step do they need instead of flaring?
notes.back: Tube fittings that eliminate all tube flaring; a new flareless tube assembly must be preset before installation.
notes.explanation: Presetting is done with the proper size presetting tool or operation.
notes.example: Like a compression fitting under a kitchen sink, where a ring bites the pipe instead of the pipe end being shaped.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Flareless Fittings”, p. 9-5
notes.evidence: Although the use of flareless tube fittings eliminates all tube flaring, another operation, referred to as presetting, is necessary prior to installation of a new flareless tube assembly.

notes.front: What is an MS flareless fitting designed for?
notes.back: Mainly high-pressure (3,000 psi) hydraulic systems that may see severe vibration or fluctuating pressure.
notes.explanation: It eliminates all tube flaring yet gives a safe, strong, dependable connection.
notes.example: Like a heavy-duty compression joint chosen for a pipe that shakes and surges.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “MS Flareless Fittings”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: MS flareless fittings are designed primarily for high-pressure (3,000 psi) hydraulic systems that may be subjected to severe vibration or fluctuating pressure.

notes.front: How is an AN flared fitting recognised?
notes.back: It has a cone at the end of the fitting; an MS flareless fitting has a straight end.
notes.explanation: The two types are different and not interchangeable.
notes.example: Like telling two plugs apart by their tips: one pointed, one flat.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “AN Flared Fittings”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: AN flared fittings are easily recognized, because they have a cone at the end of the fitting while the MS flareless fitting has a straight end.

notes.front: What are swaged fittings, and where are they used?
notes.back: Permanent, virtually maintenance-free connections, used on hydraulic lines where routine disconnection is not needed.
notes.explanation: They are often used with titanium and corrosion-resistant steel tubing and are installed with portable hydraulically powered tooling.
notes.example: Like a crimped cable end: once squeezed on, it stays until the cable is cut.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Swaged Fittings”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: Swaged fittings create a permanent connection that is virtually maintenance free. Swaged fittings are used to join hydraulic lines in areas where routine disconnections are not required

notes.front: What is a Cryofit fitting?
notes.back: A standard fitting with a cryogenic sleeve made of a shape memory alloy, Tinel.
notes.explanation: Many transport category aircraft use them on hydraulic lines where routine disconnection is not needed.
notes.example: Like a ring that is stretched while frozen and shrinks back tight as it warms.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Cryofit Fittings”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: Cryofit fittings are standard fittings with a cryogenic sleeve. The sleeve is made of a shape memory alloy, Tinel™.

notes.front: What is a bulkhead fitting, and how is it secured?
notes.back: A fitting used to secure a fluid line to a bulkhead it passes through; its longer end takes a locknut.
notes.explanation: The end that passes through the bulkhead is longer than the other end or ends.
notes.example: Like a tap connector through a sink wall, held by a nut on the far side.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Universal Bulkhead Fittings”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: The end of the fitting that passes through the bulkhead is longer than the other end(s), which allows a locknut to be installed, securing the fitting to the bulkhead.

notes.front: Why may a rigid tube be beaded?
notes.back: So a hose clamp can hold a flexible hose onto the tube.
notes.explanation: Beaded connections need a bead, a section of hose and hose clamps.
notes.example: Like the ridge on a garden tap spout that stops the hose clip sliding off.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Fittings”, p. 9-5
notes.evidence: In the case of attachment to a hose, it may be necessary to bead the rigid tube so that a clamp can be used to hold the hose onto the tube.

notes.front: What is Buna-N good for, and what must it not be used with?
notes.back: Excellent resistance to petroleum products; not for phosphate ester base hydraulic fluid (Skydrol).
notes.explanation: It is a synthetic rubber compound and must not be confused with Buna-S.
notes.example: Like a fuel hose at a petrol station: fine with petrol, the wrong choice for a Skydrol system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Buna-N”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: Buna-N is a synthetic rubber compound that has excellent resistance to petroleum products. Do not confuse with Buna-S. Do not use for phosphate ester base hydraulic fluid (Skydrol™).

notes.front: How does neoprene compare with Buna-N?
notes.back: Its resistance to petroleum products is not as good, but it has better abrasion resistance.
notes.explanation: It is an acetylene-based synthetic rubber and, like Buna-N, not for Skydrol.
notes.example: Like a tougher-skinned hose that shrugs off rubbing but is less happy soaking in fuel.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Neoprene”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: Neoprene is a synthetic rubber compound that has an acetylene base. Its resistance to petroleum products is not as good as Buna-N, but it has better abrasive resistance.

notes.front: What fluid is butyl hose excellent with, and what must it not be used with?
notes.back: Excellent with phosphate ester base hydraulic fluid (Skydrol); not to be used with petroleum products.
notes.explanation: It is a synthetic rubber made from petroleum raw materials.
notes.example: Like the reverse of a fuel hose: made for Skydrol, spoiled by petrol and oil.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Butyl”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: Butyl is a synthetic rubber compound made from petroleum raw materials. It is an excellent material to use with phosphate ester base hydraulic fluid (Skydrol™). Do not use with petroleum products.

notes.front: What is the lay line on a flexible hose?
notes.back: A marking showing the hose’s natural lay (no twist), repeated at intervals of not more than 9 inches.
notes.explanation: A lay line that spirals round an installed hose shows the hose is twisted.
notes.example: Like the stripe along a garden hose that shows at once whether it has been coiled with a twist.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Hose Identification”, p. 9-17
notes.evidence: natural lay (no twist) of the hose and are repeated at intervals of not more than 9 inches along the length of the hose.

notes.front: Where is metal tubing used, and where is flexible hose used?
notes.back: Tubing: stationary applications with long, fairly straight runs. Hose: with moving parts or where there is considerable vibration.
notes.explanation: Tubing carries fuel, oil, coolant, oxygen, instrument and hydraulic lines in many aircraft.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Fluid Lines & Fittings”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: Metal tubing (also called rigid fluid lines) is used in stationary applications and where long, relatively straight runs are possible.

notes.front: Replacement tubing should be of the same {{c1::size and material}} as the original tubing.
notes.explanation: All tubing is pressure tested before installation and designed for several times its normal operating pressure.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Fluid Lines & Fittings”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: Replacement tubing should be of the same size and material as the original tubing.

notes.front: What is 1100 or 3003 half-hard aluminium alloy tubing used for?
notes.back: General-purpose lines of low or negligible pressure, such as instrument lines and ventilating conduits.
notes.explanation: Stronger aluminium alloys are used where pressures are higher.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Aluminum Alloy Tubing”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: Tubing made from 1100 H14 (1⁄2-hard) or 3003 H14 (1⁄2-hard) is used for general purpose lines of low or negligible fluid pressures, such as instrument lines and ventilating conduits.

notes.front: What are 2024, 5052 and 6061 aluminium alloy tubing used for?
notes.back: Low- and medium-pressure systems: 1,000 to 1,500 psi hydraulic and pneumatic systems, and fuel and oil lines.
notes.explanation: These alloys come in the tempers the handbook specifies for each.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Aluminum Alloy Tubing”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: Tubing made from 2024-T3, 5052-O, and 6061-T6 aluminum alloy materials is used in general purpose systems of low and medium pressures, such as hydraulic and pneumatic 1,000 to 1,500 psi systems, and fuel and oil lines.

notes.front: Where is corrosion-resistant steel tubing used extensively?
notes.back: High-pressure hydraulic systems (3,000 psi or more) for landing gear, flaps and brakes, and in fire zones.
notes.explanation: Its higher tensile strength allows thinner walls, so it weighs little more than thicker aluminium tubing; it is also used where foreign object damage is a risk.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Steel”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: is used extensively in high-pressure hydraulic systems (3,000 psi or more) for the operation of landing gear, flaps, brakes, and in fire zones.

notes.front: Where is titanium 3AL-2.5V tubing used, and how does titanium compare with steel?
notes.back: Transport and high-performance hydraulic systems above 1,500 psi; 30 percent stronger and 50 percent lighter than steel.
notes.explanation: Cryofit or swaged fittings are used with titanium tubing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Titanium 3AL–2.5V”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: Titanium 3AL–2.5V tubing and fitting is used extensively in transport category and high-performance aircraft hydraulic systems for pressures above 1,500 psi. Titanium is 30 percent stronger than steel and 50 percent lighter than steel.

notes.front: Why must titanium tubing and fittings never be used in an oxygen system?
notes.back: Titanium is oxygen reactive: a freshly formed surface exposed to gaseous oxygen could combust spontaneously, even at low pressure.
notes.explanation: The handbook applies this to any oxygen system assembly.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Titanium 3AL–2.5V”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: Do not use titanium tubing and fittings in any oxygen system assembly. Titanium and titanium alloys are oxygen reactive. If a freshly formed titanium surface is exposed in gaseous oxygen, spontaneous combustion could occur at low pressures.

notes.front: How is the material of the original tubing positively identified?
notes.back: By comparing the code markings on the replacement tubing with the original markings on the tube being replaced.
notes.explanation: Sight tells aluminium, steel and titanium apart, but not which steel or which aluminium alloy.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Material Identification”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: To positively identify the material used in the original installation, compare code markings of the replacement tubing with the original markings on the tubing being replaced.

notes.front: How is metal tubing sized?
notes.back: By outside diameter, in sixteenths of an inch: number 6 tubing is 6/16 (3/8) inch.
notes.explanation: The tube diameter is printed on all rigid tubing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Sizes”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: Metal tubing is sized by outside diameter (OD), which is measured fractionally in sixteenths of an inch. For example, number 6 tubing is 6⁄16" (or 3⁄8")

notes.front: How is the inside diameter of a tube worked out?
notes.back: Subtract twice the wall thickness from the outside diameter.
notes.explanation: Wall thickness is printed on the tubing in thousandths of an inch, and must be known as well as material and outside diameter.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Sizes”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: The wall thickness is printed on the tubing in thousandths of an inch. To determine the inside diameter (ID) of the tube, subtract twice the wall thickness from the outside diameter.

notes.front: What four processes make up tube forming?
notes.back: Cutting, bending, flaring and beading.
notes.explanation: If a fluid line assembly is replaced, its fittings can often be salvaged, leaving only tube forming.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Fabrication of Metal Tube Lines”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: Tube forming consists of four processes: cutting, bending, flaring, and beading.

notes.front: Tubing under {{c1::1/4 inch}} in diameter usually can be bent without a bending tool.
notes.explanation: Larger sizes are usually bent with portable hand benders or production benders.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Tube Bending”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: Tubing under 1⁄4" in diameter usually can be bent without the use of a bending tool.

notes.front: How much flattening is acceptable in a tube bend?
notes.back: A small amount, provided the small diameter of the flattened part is not less than 75 percent of the original outside diameter.
notes.explanation: Excessive flattening causes fatigue failure of the tube.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Tube Bending”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: A small amount of flattening in bends is acceptable, but the small diameter of the flattened portion must not be less than 75 percent of the original outside diameter.

notes.front: What happens if a flare is made too small, or too large?
notes.back: Too small: a weak joint that may leak or pull apart. Too large: it interferes with the fitting’s threads and causes leakage.
notes.explanation: Flares are frequently subjected to extremely high pressures, so their shape must be right.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Tube Flaring”, p. 9-4
notes.evidence: A flare made too small produces a weak joint, which may leak or pull apart; if made too large, it interferes with the proper engagement of the screw thread on the fitting and causes leakage.

notes.front: What causes a crooked flare, and can extra torque fix a badly made flare?
notes.back: Tubing that was not cut squarely; no, flaws cannot be corrected by more torque on the fitting.
notes.explanation: The flare and tubing must also be free from cracks, dents, nicks and scratches.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Tube Flaring”, p. 9-4
notes.evidence: A crooked flare is the result of the tubing not being cut squarely. If a flare is not made properly, flaws cannot be corrected by applying additional torque when tightening the fitting.

notes.front: What flare angle does an aircraft flaring tool produce, and which tool is never permitted?
notes.back: 35° to 37°; an automotive-type flaring tool that produces a 45° flare is never permissible.
notes.explanation: The aircraft tool’s male and female dies are ground to produce the correct angle.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Tube Flaring”, p. 9-4
notes.evidence: The flaring tool used for aircraft tubing has male and female dies ground to produce a flare of 35° to 37°. Under no circumstance is it permissible to use an automotive-type flaring tool that produces a flare of 45°.

notes.front: On which tubing is a double flare used, and why?
notes.back: Soft aluminium alloy tubing 3/8 inch outside diameter and under, to prevent cutting off the flare and tube failure under pressure.
notes.explanation: It is smoother and more concentric than a single flare, so it seals better and resists the shearing effect of torque.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Double Flaring”, p. 9-5
notes.evidence: A double flare is used on soft aluminum alloy tubing 3⁄8" outside diameter and under. This is necessary to prevent cutting off the flare and failure of the tube assembly under operating pressures.

notes.front: When presetting a flareless fitting, how far is the nut finally tightened?
notes.back: Aluminium alloy tubing up to 1/2 inch: 1 to 1-1/6 turns. Steel, or aluminium over 1/2 inch: 1-1/6 to 1-1/2 turns.
notes.explanation: Final tightening starts once the sleeve’s cutting edge grips the tube and it no longer turns.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Flareless Fittings”, p. 9-6
notes.evidence: For aluminum alloy tubing up to and including 1⁄2" outside diameter, tighten the nut from 1 to 11⁄6 turns. For steel tubing and aluminum alloy tubing over 1⁄2" outside diameter, tighten from 11⁄6 to 11⁄2 turns.

notes.front: Aircraft fluid line markers are made up of what three elements, and what do they identify?
notes.back: Colour codes, words and geometric symbols; they identify each line’s function, content and primary hazard.
notes.explanation: The figure shows the handbook’s tape codes for each type of system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Fluid Line Identification”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: Fluid lines in aircraft are often identified by markers made up of color codes, words, and geometric symbols. These markers identify each line’s function, content, and primary hazard.

image.alt: Fifteen fluid line identification tapes, each repeating a system name on a colour field, most with a geometric symbol column: fuel, lubrication, pneumatic, hydraulic, coolant, air condition, electrical conduit, water, compressed gas, instrument air, breathing oxygen, fire protection, de-icing, vacuum and inerting fluid. A sixteenth panel shows the skull-and-crossbones warning symbol.
image.credit: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), Figure 9-16

notes.front: Instead of tape or decals, when are steel tags or paint used to mark fluid lines?
notes.back: Tags: on lines 4 inches or larger, lines in oily environments, hot lines and some cold lines. Paint: in engine compartments.
notes.explanation: In engine compartments, tapes, decals or tags could be drawn into the engine induction system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Fluid Line Identification”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: On lines 4" in diameter (or larger), lines in oily environment, hot lines, and on some cold lines, steel tags may be used in place of tape or decals. [Figure 9-17B] Paint is used on lines in engine compartments

notes.front: Which hazard markings may be added to fuel lines, lines with toxic materials, and lines with physically dangerous materials?
notes.back: Fuel: `FLAM`. Toxic materials: `TOXIC`. Physically dangerous materials such as oxygen or nitrogen: `PHDAN`.
notes.explanation: Lines may also be marked for function, such as drain, vent, pressure or return.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Fluid Line Identification”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: Lines conveying fuel may be marked FLAM [Figure 9-17]; lines containing toxic materials are marked TOXIC in place of FLAM. Lines containing physically dangerous materials, such as oxygen, nitrogen, or FreonTM, may be marked PHDAN.

notes.front: How do pipe-thread fittings seal, and what caution applies to oxygen lines?
notes.back: The tapered threads form the seal; no lubricants may be used on oxygen lines.
notes.explanation: Oxygen reacts with petroleum products and can ignite.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Fluid Line End Fittings”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: When two fittings are joined, a male into a female, the thread taper forms a seal.

notes.front: Do machine threads seal a fitting the way tapered pipe threads do, and what makes such a connection fluid-tight?
notes.back: No; a flared tube connection, a crush washer or a synthetic seal makes it fluid-tight.
notes.explanation: Machine threads have no taper; they only draw connections together or attach through bulkheads.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Fluid Line End Fittings”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: A flared tube connection, a crush washer, or a synthetic seal is used to make the connection fluid tight. Machine threads have no taper and do not form a fluid-tight seal.

notes.front: What does the dash number of a machine-thread fitting give?
notes.back: The nominal outside diameter, in sixteenths of an inch.
notes.explanation: It matches the way tubing itself is sized.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Fluid Line End Fittings”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: The size of these fittings is given in dash numbers, which equal the nominal outside diameter in sixteenths of an inch.

notes.front: What are the four types of fitting that attach tubing to tubing or to system units?
notes.back: Bead and clamp; flared; flareless; and permanent fittings.
notes.explanation: System pressure and the material used usually decide which connector is chosen.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Fittings”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: There are four types: (1) bead and clamp, (2) flared fittings, (3) flareless fittings, and (4) permanent fittings

notes.front: In which systems may beaded fittings be used, compared with flared, flareless and permanent fittings?
notes.back: Beaded: only low- or medium-pressure systems such as vacuum and coolant. The others: all systems, regardless of pressure.
notes.explanation: A beaded fitting needs a bead, a section of hose and hose clamps.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Fittings”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: is used only in low- or mediumpressure systems, such as vacuum and coolant systems. The flared, flareless, or permanent-type fittings may be used as connectors in all systems, regardless of the pressure.

notes.front: In a parts bin, a mechanic finds a black AN fitting. What is it made of?
notes.back: A) Steel
notes.choices:
A) Steel
B) Aluminium bronze
C) Brass
D) Aluminium
notes.choicesExplained: D: AN aluminium fittings are blue. B: aluminium bronze fittings are cadmium plated and natural in appearance. C: brass is not given a colour in this scheme.
notes.explanation: Standard AN fittings are identified by their black or blue colour, and all steel ones are black.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “AN Flared Fittings”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: All AN steel fittings are colored black, all AN aluminum fittings are colored blue, and aluminum bronze fittings are cadmium plated and natural in appearance.

notes.front: Why must compound never be applied to the faces of a fitting or flare?
notes.back: It destroys the metal-to-metal contact between fitting and flare that produces the seal.
notes.explanation: Also align the line before tightening; never pull it into place with torque on the nut.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Connection & Torque”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: Never apply compound to the faces of the fitting or the flare, as it destroys the metal-to-metal contact between the fitting and flare, a contact which is necessary to produce the seal.

notes.front: What can overtightening and undertightening a tube fitting each cause?
notes.back: Over: a damaged or cut-off flare, or a ruined sleeve or nut. Under: the line may blow out or leak under pressure.
notes.explanation: Torque wrenches and the prescribed torque values prevent both.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Connection & Torque”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: Failure to tighten sufficiently also may be serious, as this condition may allow the line to blow out of the assembly or to leak under system pressure. The use of torque wrenches and the prescribed torque values prevents overtightening or undertightening.

notes.front: When installing a flareless fitting, where does final tightening start, and how far is the nut turned?
notes.back: Where the nut just begins to bottom; then one-sixth turn (one flat on the hex).
notes.explanation: A wrench on the connector stops it turning while the nut is tightened.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Flareless Tube Installation”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: It is important that the final tightening commence at the point where the nut just begins to bottom. Use a wrench and turn the nut one-sixth turn (one flat on a hex nut).

notes.front: A flareless tube nut must never be tightened beyond {{c1::one-third turn (two flats on the hex nut)}}.
notes.explanation: That is the most the fitting can take without possibly damaging the sleeve and nut permanently.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Flareless Tube Installation”, p. 9-14
notes.evidence: Never tighten the nut beyond one-third turn (two flats on the hex nut); this is the maximum the fitting may be tightened without the possibility of permanently damaging the sleeve and nut.

notes.front: Which scratches or nicks in aluminium alloy tubing may be repaired by burnishing?
notes.back: Those not deeper than 10 percent of the wall thickness and not in the heel of a bend.
notes.explanation: Limits for hard, thin-walled steel and titanium tubing are considerably less; consult the maintenance manual.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Rigid Tubing Inspection & Repair”, p. 9-14
notes.evidence: Scratches or nicks not deeper than 10 percent of the wall thickness in aluminum alloy tubing, which are not in the heel of a bend, may be repaired by burnishing with hand tools.

notes.front: How large a dent in tubing is not objectionable?
notes.back: Less than 20 percent of the tube diameter, unless it is in the heel of a bend.
notes.explanation: Dents can be removed by drawing a bullet of the right size through the tube.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Rigid Tubing Inspection & Repair”, p. 9-14
notes.evidence: A dent of less than 20 percent of the tube diameter is not objectionable, unless it is in the heel of a bend.

notes.front: Any crack or deformity in a flare is {{c1::unacceptable and cause for rejection}}.
notes.explanation: Lines with severe die marks, seams or splits are also replaced.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Rigid Tubing Inspection & Repair”, p. 9-14
notes.evidence: Replace lines with severe die marks, seams, or splits in the tube. Any crack or deformity in a flare is unacceptable and is cause for rejection.

notes.front: Why should a replacement tube never follow a path with no bends?
notes.back: A tube cannot be cut or flared accurately enough to fit straight without strain; bends also allow for temperature change and vibration.
notes.explanation: The new tube should never need pulling into alignment with its coupling nuts.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Rigid Tubing Installation and Inspection”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: A tube cannot be cut or flared accurately enough so that it can be installed without bending and still be free from mechanical strain. Bends are also necessary to permit the tubing to expand or contract under temperature changes and to absorb vibration.

notes.front: In AC 43.13-1B, what should metal hydraulic lines be checked for?
notes.back: Leaks, loose anchorage, scratches, kinks or other damage.
notes.explanation: Fittings are checked for leakage, looseness, cracks and burrs, and lines must not chafe against one another.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Inspection and Repair, Chapter 9, paragraph 9-30, Hydraulic Lines and Fittings
notes.evidence: Check metal lines for leaks, loose anchorage, scratches, kinks, or other damage. Inspect fittings and connections for leakage, looseness, cracks, burrs, or other damage.

notes.front: What operating temperature range does Teflon hose have?
notes.explanation: Teflon is compatible with nearly every substance used and has practically limitless shelf and service life.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Hose Materials & Construction”, p. 9-17
notes.evidence: It has a broad operating temperature range (−65 °F to +450 °F). It is compatible with nearly every substance or agent used.

notes.front: What pressure defines low-pressure hose, and how is it reinforced?
notes.back: Below 250 psi; fabric braid reinforcement.
notes.explanation: Hose types are classified by the pressure they are designed to withstand in normal operation.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Hose Materials & Construction”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: Low pressure—below 250 psi. Fabric braid reinforcement.

notes.front: What pressures does medium-pressure hose carry, and how is it reinforced?
notes.back: Up to 3,000 psi in smaller sizes and up to 1,500 psi in larger sizes; one wire braid.
notes.explanation: The limit depends on the hose size.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Hose Materials & Construction”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: Medium pressure—up to 3,000 psi. One wire braid reinforcement. Smaller sizes carry up to 3,000 psi. Larger sizes carry pressure up to 1,500 psi.

notes.front: High-pressure hose is rated, in all sizes, for up to {{c1::3,000 psi}} operating pressure.
notes.explanation: Unlike medium-pressure hose, its rating does not drop in larger sizes.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Hose Materials & Construction”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: High pressure—all sizes up to 3,000 psi operating pressures.

notes.front: What do the markings on most hydraulic hose identify?
notes.back: Its type, the quarter and year of manufacture, and a 5-digit code identifying the manufacturer.
notes.explanation: Code markings help replace a hose with one of the same specification or an approved substitute.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Hose Identification”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: Most hydraulic hose is marked to identify its type, the quarter and year of manufacture, and a 5-digit code identifying the manufacturer.

notes.front: What are three signs of flexible hose deterioration that call for replacement?
notes.back: Any three of: leakage; cover or braid separating; cracks; hardening; lack of flexibility; excessive cold flow.
notes.explanation: Hose is checked for deterioration at each inspection period.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Flexible Hose Inspection”, p. 9-18
notes.evidence: Leakage, separation of the cover or braid from the inner tube, cracks, hardening, lack of flexibility, or excessive “cold flow” are apparent signs of deterioration and reason for replacement.

notes.front: What does “cold flow” describe in a flexible hose?
notes.back: Deep, permanent impressions in the hose made by the pressure of hose clamps or supports.
notes.explanation: Excessive cold flow is a sign of deterioration and a reason to replace the hose.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Flexible Hose Inspection”, p. 9-18
notes.evidence: The term “cold flow” describes the deep, permanent impressions in the hose produced by the pressure of hose clamps or supports.

notes.front: A hose assembly with swaged end fittings has failed. The shop has bulk hose and reusable fittings. What should be done?
notes.back: B) Replace the entire assembly with a new factory-made one of the correct size and length
notes.choices:
A) Cut off the swaged ends and fit reusable fittings to new hose
B) Replace the entire assembly with a new factory-made one of the correct size and length
C) Clamp a repair sleeve over the failure
D) Re-swage the old fittings onto new hose in the shop
notes.choicesExplained: A and D treat the assembly as rebuildable, but swaged assemblies are made and tested at the factory. C is not a repair the handbook gives.
notes.explanation: Only hose with reusable end fittings can be refabricated in the shop.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Flexible Hose Inspection”, p. 9-18
notes.evidence: When failure occurs in a flexible hose equipped with swaged end fittings, the entire assembly must be replaced. Obtain a new hose assembly of the correct size and length, complete with factory installed end fittings.

notes.front: How is a flexible hose assembly proof-tested with gas, and to what pressure is a repaired hose recommended to be tested?
notes.back: Gas tests are conducted underwater; a repaired or overhauled hose to at least 1.5 times system pressure.
notes.explanation: All flexible hose must be proof-tested after assembly, following the hose maker’s instructions.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Testing of Flexible Hose Assemblies”, p. 9-19
notes.evidence: Hose tests, using a gas, are conducted underwater.

notes.front: What does a hose’s dash number indicate?
notes.back: The size of tubing the hose is compatible with, not its inside or outside diameter.
notes.explanation: When the hose’s dash number matches the tubing’s, the hose is the proper size.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Size Designations”, p. 9-19
notes.evidence: The dash number is stenciled on the side of the hose and indicates the size tubing with which the hose is compatible. It does not denote inside or outside diameter.

notes.front: How much slack should be left in a flexible hose, and why?
notes.back: 5 to 8 percent of its total length, for changes in length when pressure is applied.
notes.explanation: Flexible hose contracts in length and expands in diameter when pressurised.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Slack”, p. 9-21
notes.evidence: When installing flexible hose, provide slack or bend in the hose line from 5 to 8 percent of its total length to provide for changes in length that occurs when pressure is applied. Flexible hose contracts in length and expands in diameter when pressurized.

notes.front: Near its end fittings, how must a hose be installed?
notes.back: So flexure does not occur at the end fittings: straight for at least two hose diameters from them.
notes.explanation: The metal end fittings are not flexible, and clamps should not restrict hose flexing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Flex”, p. 9-21
notes.evidence: Install the hose so that flexure does not occur at the end fittings. The hose must remain straight for at least two hose diameters from the end fittings.

notes.front: Why must hoses be installed without twisting, and what relieves twist stresses?
notes.back: Twisting may rupture the hose or loosen the attaching nuts; swivel connections at one or both ends relieve it.
notes.explanation: Twisting shows on the identification stripe running along the hose, which should not spiral.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Twisting”, p. 9-21
notes.evidence: Hoses must be installed without twisting to avoid possible rupture of the hose or loosening of the attaching nuts. Use of swivel connections at one or both ends relieve twist stresses.

notes.front: A new hose route would force a bend tighter than the hose’s recommended minimum radius. What should the mechanic do?
notes.back: A) Use an elbow fitting or elbow-type end fitting to avoid the sharp bend
notes.choices:
A) Use an elbow fitting or elbow-type end fitting to avoid the sharp bend
B) Clamp the bend tightly to hold it
C) Twist the hose to ease the bend
D) Install it: pressure will straighten it
notes.choicesExplained: D ignores that sharp bends cut bursting pressure well below the rating. B restricts flexing and does not ease the bend. C adds a twist, which may rupture the hose.
notes.explanation: Bends that are too sharp reduce a hose’s bursting pressure considerably.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Bend Radius”, p. 9-21
notes.evidence: To avoid sharp bends in the hose assembly, use elbow fittings, hose with elbow-type end fittings, or the appropriate bend radii. Bends that are too sharp reduce the bursting pressure of flexible hose considerably below its rated value.

notes.front: Flexible hose must be supported at least every {{c1::24 inches}}, and closer supports are desirable.
notes.explanation: Hose must also clear all other lines, equipment and structure under every operating condition.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Clearance”, p. 9-21
notes.evidence: Although hose must be supported at least every 24 inches, closer supports are desirable. Flexible hose must never be stretched tightly between two fittings.

notes.front: What calibrations do hose clamp torque-limiting wrenches come in, and what is used without one?
notes.back: 15 and 25 in-lb; without one, the finger-tight-plus-turns method.
notes.explanation: The finger-tight values are approximate, so good judgement is needed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Hose Clamps”, p. 9-22
notes.evidence: These wrenches are available in calibrations of 15 and 25 in-lb limits. In the absence of torque-limiting wrenches, follow the finger-tightplus-turns method.

notes.front: A coolant hose clamp was correctly tightened yesterday. What should be done over the next several days, and why?
notes.back: Recheck its tightness; hose connections undergo cold flow, a setting process.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls for a follow-up tightening check for several days after installation.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Hose Clamps”, p. 9-22
notes.evidence: Since hose connections are subject to “cold flow” or a setting process, a follow-up tightening check should be made for several days after installation.

notes.front: After installing critical fluid hose and line fittings, what do the mechanic certification standards expect applicants to understand?
notes.back: The importance of using a torque wrench, and the use of torque seal or similar witness techniques.
notes.explanation: A witness mark over a fitting makes later movement or loosening visible.
notes.source: FAA-S-ACS-1, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards, Area of Operation I, Task D (Fluid Lines and Fittings), AM.I.D.K5 and K6, p. 11
notes.evidence: Importance of using a torque wrench when securing fluid hose and line fittings. AM.I.D.K6 Use of torque seal or similar witness techniques after installing critical fluid hose and line fittings.

notes.front: A mechanic needs number 12 tubing. What outside diameter is that?
notes.back: D) 3/4 inch
notes.choices:
A) 12/32 inch
B) 12 millimetres
C) 1/2 inch
D) 3/4 inch
notes.choicesExplained: B uses the wrong unit entirely. C is number 8 tubing. A uses thirty-seconds instead of sixteenths.
notes.explanation: Tube numbers are sixteenths of an inch of outside diameter: 12/16 = 3/4.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Sizes”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: Metal tubing is sized by outside diameter (OD), which is measured fractionally in sixteenths of an inch.

notes.front: A number 8 tube has a wall thickness of 0.035 inch. What is its inside diameter?
notes.explanation: Number 8 is 8/16, or 0.500 inch, outside diameter.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Sizes”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: To determine the inside diameter (ID) of the tube, subtract twice the wall thickness from the outside diameter.

notes.front: The only flaring tool in the hangar is an automotive one that makes a 45° flare. May it be used on an aircraft brake line?
notes.back: B) No, never: aircraft flares are 35° to 37°
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if the fitting is torqued harder
B) No, never: aircraft flares are 35° to 37°
C) Yes, if the flare is inspected afterwards
D) Yes, for low-pressure lines only
notes.choicesExplained: A fails because extra torque cannot correct a flawed flare. D and C invent exceptions the handbook does not allow.
notes.explanation: The handbook says under no circumstance may an automotive 45° tool be used.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Tube Flaring”, p. 9-4
notes.evidence: Under no circumstance is it permissible to use an automotive-type flaring tool that produces a flare of 45°.

notes.front: A 1/4 inch soft aluminium alloy line must be flared for a pressure system. Which flare is called for?
notes.back: D) A double flare
notes.choices:
A) A single flare with extra torque
B) A single 45° flare
C) No flare: use a beaded joint
D) A double flare
notes.choicesExplained: B uses a forbidden angle. C suits only low- or medium-pressure hose joints. A relies on torque, which cannot fix flare problems.
notes.explanation: Double flares are used on soft aluminium alloy tubing 3/8 inch outside diameter and under.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Double Flaring”, p. 9-5
notes.evidence: A double flare is used on soft aluminum alloy tubing 3⁄8" outside diameter and under.

notes.front: To save weight, someone proposes titanium tubing for an oxygen system line. What is the right response?
notes.back: D) Reject it: titanium must not be used in any oxygen system
notes.choices:
A) Accept it: titanium is lighter and stronger than steel
B) Accept it if the pressure is low
C) Accept it with Cryofit fittings
D) Reject it: titanium must not be used in any oxygen system
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the oxygen hazard. B fails because combustion could occur even at low pressures. C changes the fittings, not the material hazard.
notes.explanation: Titanium is oxygen reactive and can combust spontaneously in gaseous oxygen.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Titanium 3AL–2.5V”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: Do not use titanium tubing and fittings in any oxygen system assembly.

notes.front: A line in a 3,000 psi landing gear hydraulic system near the wheel well needs replacing. Which tubing material fits the handbook’s description?
notes.back: C) Corrosion-resistant steel
notes.choices:
A) 3003 half-hard aluminium alloy
B) Copper
C) Corrosion-resistant steel
D) 1100 half-hard aluminium alloy
notes.choicesExplained: A and D are for low or negligible pressures. B has generally been replaced in modern aircraft.
notes.explanation: Corrosion-resistant steel is used in 3,000 psi systems for landing gear and where foreign object damage is a risk.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Steel”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: Steel lines are used where there is a risk of foreign object damage (FOD) (i.e., the landing gear and wheel well areas).

notes.front: A mechanic cannot tell by eye whether an aluminium line is 5052 or 6061 alloy. How should the replacement be matched?
notes.back: B) Compare the code markings on the new tubing with those on the old
notes.choices:
A) Pick the harder alloy to be safe
B) Compare the code markings on the new tubing with those on the old
C) Use steel instead
D) Match the colour of the paint on the aircraft
notes.choicesExplained: A and C ignore that replacement tubing should match the original. D confuses aircraft paint with tube colour codes.
notes.explanation: Code markings positively identify the material; hardness testing is a fallback if they cannot be read.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Material Identification”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: To positively identify the material used in the original installation, compare code markings of the replacement tubing with the original markings on the tubing being replaced.

notes.front: A bend in 1/2 inch tubing measures 0.360 inch across its flattest part. Is it acceptable?
notes.back: No. 75 percent of 0.500 is 0.375 inch, and 0.360 is below that.
notes.explanation: The flattened diameter must not be less than 75 percent of the original outside diameter.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Tube Bending”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: the small diameter of the flattened portion must not be less than 75 percent of the original outside diameter.

notes.front: A newly made flare sits crooked and the joint weeps under test. What is the correct action?
notes.back: B) Cut the tube square and remake the flare
notes.choices:
A) Tighten the nut further until the leak stops
B) Cut the tube square and remake the flare
C) Apply sealing compound to the flare face
D) Add a second sleeve
notes.choicesExplained: A fails because extra torque cannot correct a badly made flare. C destroys the metal-to-metal seal. D is not a method the handbook gives.
notes.explanation: A crooked flare comes from tubing that was not cut squarely.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Tube Flaring”, p. 9-4
notes.evidence: A crooked flare is the result of the tubing not being cut squarely. If a flare is not made properly, flaws cannot be corrected by applying additional torque when tightening the fitting.

notes.front: A flared joint seeps slightly. A colleague suggests smearing thread compound on the flare face before retightening. What is the right response?
notes.back: A) Refuse: compound on the flare face destroys the metal-to-metal seal
notes.choices:
A) Refuse: compound on the flare face destroys the metal-to-metal seal
B) Agree, if only a thin film is used
C) Use compound on the nut threads and flare face both
D) Agree: compound improves any seal
notes.choicesExplained: D and B still put compound where the seal is made. C adds compound to the flare face as well.
notes.explanation: The seal depends on metal-to-metal contact between fitting and flare.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Connection & Torque”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: Never apply compound to the faces of the fitting or the flare, as it destroys the metal-to-metal contact between the fitting and flare, a contact which is necessary to produce the seal.

notes.front: A flareless fitting, tightened one-sixth turn past bottoming, leaks under pressure test. What is next?
notes.back: D) Tighten one more sixth (one-third in total); if it still leaks, remove and inspect
notes.choices:
A) Tighten until the leak stops, however far
B) Back the nut off one-sixth turn
C) Replace the tube immediately
D) Tighten one more sixth (one-third in total); if it still leaks, remove and inspect
notes.choicesExplained: A risks going past the one-third-turn maximum. C skips the permitted extra tightening. B loosens a leaking joint.
notes.explanation: Beyond one-third turn the sleeve and nut may be permanently damaged.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Flareless Tube Installation”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: It is permissible to tighten the nut an additional one-sixth turn (making a total of one-third turn), should a connection leak.

notes.front: An aluminium alloy line with a 0.049 inch wall has a 0.004 inch scratch on a straight section. What does the handbook allow?
notes.back: D) Repair it by burnishing with hand tools
notes.choices:
A) Replace the line
B) Nothing: scratches never matter
C) Fill it with sealant
D) Repair it by burnishing with hand tools
notes.choicesExplained: A is not required: the scratch is within limits. C is not a listed repair. B ignores that deeper scratches or ones in a bend heel need other action.
notes.explanation: 0.004 is about 8 percent of 0.049, within the 10 percent limit and not in the heel of a bend.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Rigid Tubing Inspection & Repair”, p. 9-14
notes.evidence: Scratches or nicks not deeper than 10 percent of the wall thickness in aluminum alloy tubing, which are not in the heel of a bend, may be repaired by burnishing with hand tools.

notes.front: A tube has a dent of 15 percent of its diameter at the heel of a bend. Is it acceptable under the 20 percent rule?
notes.back: D) No: the 20 percent allowance does not apply in the heel of a bend
notes.choices:
A) Only on steel tubing
B) Yes: it is under 20 percent
C) Yes, if burnished
D) No: the 20 percent allowance does not apply in the heel of a bend
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the heel-of-bend exception. C confuses the scratch repair with dent limits. A invents a material condition.
notes.explanation: A dent under 20 percent is not objectionable unless it is in the heel of a bend.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Rigid Tubing Inspection & Repair”, p. 9-14
notes.evidence: A dent of less than 20 percent of the tube diameter is not objectionable, unless it is in the heel of a bend.

notes.front: A hose is needed for a system using phosphate ester base hydraulic fluid (Skydrol). Which synthetic rubber is the right choice?
notes.back: C) Butyl
notes.choices:
A) Buna-N
B) Neoprene
C) Butyl
D) Pure rubber
notes.choicesExplained: A and B must not be used with Skydrol. D is never used in flexible fluid lines.
notes.explanation: Butyl is an excellent material for phosphate ester base hydraulic fluid.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Butyl”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: It is an excellent material to use with phosphate ester base hydraulic fluid (Skydrol™). Do not use with petroleum products.

notes.front: A hose will carry petroleum-based fuel. Of these, which synthetic rubber has excellent petroleum resistance?
notes.back: A) Buna-N
notes.choices:
A) Buna-N
B) Butyl
C) Buna-S
D) Pure rubber
notes.choicesExplained: B must not be used with petroleum products. C is a different compound the handbook warns not to confuse with Buna-N. D is never used.
notes.explanation: Buna-N has excellent resistance to petroleum products.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Buna-N”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: Buna-N is a synthetic rubber compound that has excellent resistance to petroleum products. Do not confuse with Buna-S.

notes.front: A large-size hose must carry 2,500 psi. Which pressure class does it need?
notes.back: B) High pressure
notes.choices:
A) Low pressure
B) High pressure
C) Medium pressure
D) Any class
notes.choicesExplained: A is below 250 psi. C in larger sizes carries only up to 1,500 psi. D ignores the ratings.
notes.explanation: High-pressure hose carries up to 3,000 psi in all sizes.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Hose Materials & Construction”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: High pressure—all sizes up to 3,000 psi operating pressures.

notes.front: A hose is to connect to -8 tubing. What hose dash number is needed?
notes.back: A -8 hose.
notes.explanation: Hose dash numbers give the compatible tubing size, not the hose’s own diameters.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Size Designations”, p. 9-19
notes.evidence: When the dash number of the hose corresponds with the dash number of the tubing, the proper size hose is being used.

notes.front: A flexible hose run is 50 inches long. How much slack should be provided?
notes.back: 2.5 to 4 inches (5 to 8 percent of 50).
notes.explanation: The slack allows for the hose shortening when pressurised.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Slack”, p. 9-21
notes.evidence: provide slack or bend in the hose line from 5 to 8 percent of its total length

notes.front: After installing a hose, a mechanic sees its lay line spiralling around it. What does this show, and what is done?
notes.back: D) The hose is twisted; reinstall it without twist
notes.choices:
A) The hose is the wrong colour; replace it
B) Normal; lay lines always spiral
C) The hose is too short; stretch it tight
D) The hose is twisted; reinstall it without twist
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the stripe should not spiral. C is forbidden: hose must never be stretched tight. A misreads the marking.
notes.explanation: Twisting may rupture the hose or loosen its nuts, and a spiralling stripe reveals it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Twisting”, p. 9-21
notes.evidence: Twisting of the hose can be determined from the identification

notes.front: At inspection, a hose shows deep permanent dents under its clamps and has lost flexibility. What should be done?
notes.back: B) Replace the hose
notes.choices:
A) Tighten the clamps
B) Replace the hose
C) Move the clamps to a new place
D) Leave it until it leaks
notes.choicesExplained: A adds more clamp pressure. D waits for a failure. C leaves a deteriorated hose in service.
notes.explanation: Excessive cold flow and lack of flexibility are signs of deterioration and reason for replacement.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Flexible Hose Inspection”, p. 9-18
notes.evidence: lack of flexibility, or excessive “cold flow” are apparent signs of deterioration and reason for replacement.

notes.front: A fuel line in an engine compartment needs its identification marking replaced. What marking method does the handbook give?
notes.back: D) Paint
notes.choices:
A) A steel tag
B) 1-inch tape
C) A decal
D) Paint
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and A could be drawn into the engine induction system.
notes.explanation: Paint is used on lines in engine compartments for that reason.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Fluid Line Identification”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: Paint is used on lines in engine compartments where there is the possibility of tapes, decals, or tags being drawn into the engine induction system.

notes.front: A mechanic has torqued a critical hydraulic line fitting. What should follow, per the mechanic certification standards?
notes.back: A) Apply torque seal or a similar witness mark
notes.choices:
A) Apply torque seal or a similar witness mark
B) Paint the whole fitting
C) Loosen it slightly for thermal growth
D) Nothing further
notes.choicesExplained: B hides the fitting rather than witnessing it. C creates the loosened-fitting risk the standards list. D skips the witness technique.
notes.explanation: The standards also list a loosened fitting as a risk to manage.
notes.source: FAA-S-ACS-1, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards, Area of Operation I, Task D (Fluid Lines and Fittings), AM.I.D.K6 and R6, p. 11
notes.evidence: Use of torque seal or similar witness techniques after installing critical fluid hose and line fittings.

notes.front: Can AN flared fittings and MS flareless fittings be interchanged?
notes.back: No. They are different and not interchangeable.
notes.explanation: The AN fitting has a cone at its end; the MS flareless fitting has a straight end.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “AN Flared Fittings”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: AN flared fittings are different from MS flareless fittings and they are not interchangeable.

notes.front: Buna-N or butyl: which suits petroleum products, and which suits Skydrol?
notes.back: Buna-N suits petroleum products; butyl suits Skydrol. Each must not be used with the other fluid.
notes.explanation: The two synthetic rubbers have opposite fluid compatibilities.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Hose Materials & Construction”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: Butyl is a synthetic rubber compound made from petroleum raw materials. It is an excellent material to use with phosphate ester base hydraulic fluid (Skydrol™). Do not use with petroleum products.

notes.front: How is a failed Cryofit fitting replaced without replacing the whole hydraulic line?
notes.back: Cut the tube at the sleeve; this leaves room to fit a swaged fitting instead.
notes.explanation: Both are permanent fittings that are removed only by cutting.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 9, Fluid Lines & Fittings, “Cryofit Fittings”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: Cryofit fittings can only be removed by cutting the tube at the sleeve, though this leaves enough room to replace it with a swaged fitting without replacing the hydraulic line.
